title: Grease waste, runoff and environmental controls
audience: Cleaners and supervisors handling greasy waste and washwater from commercial kitchen exhaust work.
learningOutcomes: Recognise grease residues and greasy washwater as fire and contamination hazards.
Identify approved waste handling and wastewater protections.
Stop an unapproved discharge, and route waste decisions to the site operator and a lawful waste contractor.

instruction.heading: Where the grease goes
instruction.body: Kitchen exhaust cleaning removes a material that has been building up for a long time. It is oily, it contains food residue, and it is often mixed with detergent and hot water when it is loosened. Every step of the job creates a waste stream: the grease scraped from a canopy, the saturated filter wash, the rinse water that runs down a drain, the rags and absorbent material, and the containers that hold the residue until it is collected. Each stream has its own risk. Grease that is left in a bin near a heat source is a fire risk. Washwater that enters a stormwater grate reaches the environment without treatment. Greasy washwater that enters a sewer without the right pre-treatment can block pipes and breach trade waste conditions. The job is therefore not finished when the surface is clean. It is finished when every waste stream has been handled, stored and recorded in a way the site operator has approved.

instruction.heading: Fire and contamination hazards of greasy waste
instruction.body: NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant guidance identifies the ignition of fatty residue in hoods and ducting as a risk, and the same logic applies to waste that has been removed from the system but is still oily. Keep greasy waste in closed, labelled containers, away from cooking equipment, heat sources and electrical outlets, and out of direct sun. Do not store rags soaked in grease in a pile. Do not leave a bucket of greasy washwater standing near an open flame or a fryer exhaust. The fire hazard is the reason for the storage rule, and the contamination hazard is the reason for the discharge rule. Both are the site operator's responsibility to control, and the cleaner's responsibility to report when they see a breach.

instruction.heading: Trade waste and approved pre-treatment
instruction.body: Greasy washwater from a food premises may be a regulated trade waste, depending on the premises and the utility. Trade waste rules are set by the water authority or the council that serves the premises, and the rules differ between utilities. Sydney Water's published guidance for food businesses states that a grease trap or arrestor should be sized to the maximum hourly flow, installed by a licensed plumber, fitted with the lid or cover the manufacturer specifies, and kept with overhead clearance at least equal to its deepest part so that it can be cleaned and inspected safely. The same guidance says that unlisted pre-treatment products may have to be removed. That guidance does not say who must maintain the unit, and it gives no cleaning or pump-out frequency. For this lesson, the principle is that a pre-treatment device is a protection that must not be bypassed, blocked or opened by a cleaner without the site's authority. Where a trade waste approval or a pre-treatment requirement applies at a site, it is recorded in the site file.

instruction.heading: Stopping an unapproved discharge
instruction.body: A cleaner who sees greasy water heading for a stormwater grate, a floor drain that is not connected to pre-treatment, or a neighbour's yard should stop the discharge at its source if it is safe to do so. Use absorbent material, sealed containers and drip trays to contain the flow. Do not pour water, detergent or degreaser down any drain to clear the path. Do not add more product to 'dilute' the water. Tell the supervisor and the site operator at once. Record the time, the location, what was seen, what was done to contain it, and who was told. The decision about the discharge route, the treatment and any notification to the utility or the regulator belongs to the site operator and, where applicable, the regulator. It does not belong to the cleaner, and it is not decided by the cheapest contractor on the day.

instruction.heading: Lawful waste handling and the record
instruction.body: Greasy waste leaves the site through a waste contractor who is authorised to collect and transport it. Confirm the contractor's details before the waste is loaded, and keep a record of the collection with the date, the quantity or number of containers, the contractor's name, the destination and the person who signed for it. State requirements for waste transport and for tracking regulated wastes differ between jurisdictions, and this lesson does not confirm them. Where a state requirement applies, the site operator must confirm it before the first collection. The cleaner's part is to keep the containers sealed, labelled and separated by stream, to hand over only to the approved contractor, and to keep the record that proves it.

procedure: Identify each waste stream produced by the job: scraped grease, saturated filter wash, rinse water, rags and absorbent material, and containers.
Check the site's waste and wastewater instructions, including any trade waste approval or pre-treatment requirement, before the job starts.
Keep greasy waste in closed, labelled containers, away from heat sources and electrical outlets, and separated by stream.
Confirm that no greasy washwater is directed to a stormwater grate, an unconnected drain or a neighbouring property.
If an unapproved discharge is seen, stop it at source if safe, contain it with absorbent material, and tell the supervisor and site operator at once.
Hand over waste only to the contractor the site operator has approved, and confirm the contractor's details before loading.
Record the waste streams, the containers, the time of each handover, the contractor and the person who signed.

workedExamples.situation: A subcontractor, working at the back of a takeaway shop, wants to drain the greasy washwater from a canopy clean into the stormwater grate in the lane, because the floor drain is blocked and the bucket is heavy.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and who decides the route?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not drain the water into the stormwater grate. Stop the discharge, contain the water with absorbent material, and keep the bucket closed. Tell the supervisor and the site operator at once, and record the time, the location and the containment. The site operator decides the route for the water, which may be through the approved pre-treatment, a licensed collection or another method approved for the site. The cleaner does not decide the route.

workedExamples.situation: At the end of a shift, a bin of greasy rags and a sealed drum of greasy scrapings are left next to the fryer exhaust while you wait for the collection truck, which is due the next day.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the storage acceptable, and what do you change?
workedExamples.reasoning: The storage is not acceptable. Greasy material near a fryer or other heat source is a fire risk. Move the containers to the site's approved storage place away from cooking equipment and outlets, close the lids, and label them. Tell the site operator that storage was not set up correctly and record the move and the time. Confirm the collection date with the approved contractor.

equipmentAndPpe: Closed, labelled containers for scraped grease and greasy washwater, separated by stream.
Absorbent material and a spill kit approved by the site, with a container for used absorbent.
Drip trays or ground covers where the site requires them.
Waste collection record sheet, with contractor details and signatures.

PPE as set by the product safety data sheet and the site risk assessment. Gloves, eye protection and closed footwear are typical starting points for greasy work (lesson practice, not a sourced requirement); the sheet and the risk assessment decide the final PPE.

commonErrors.error: Draining greasy washwater into a stormwater grate or an unconnected drain because the normal drain is blocked.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop the discharge, contain the water, and tell the site operator. The route is the site operator's decision.

commonErrors.error: Storing greasy waste near a fryer or other heat source while waiting for collection.
commonErrors.prevention: Move it to the approved storage place away from heat sources and outlets, with lids closed and labels on.

commonErrors.error: Adding detergent or degreaser to a drain to clear a greasy blockage.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not add product to a drain. Report the blockage and let the site operator decide the method.

commonErrors.error: Handing waste to a collector without confirming its authority.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the contractor's details against the site's approved list before loading, and record the handover.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant guidance identifies the ignition of fatty residue in hoods and ducting as a fire risk. This lesson applies the same logic to greasy waste held on site. The guidance is NSW only.

Sydney Water's guidance on pre-treatment for food businesses says a licensed plumber must install a grease trap or arrestor, that the lid or cover must be the one specified by the manufacturer, and that clearance above the trap must allow cleaning and inspection. The guidance does not state who maintains the unit or how often it is cleaned.
A safety data sheet must cover safe handling, including disposal, for each hazardous product used. Keep the sheet for every product in the waste stream, and follow its disposal statements.
Do not transport or dispose of waste as a cleaner unless the site operator confirms the lawful route in writing.

This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority. Pre-treatment installation, waste transport and wastewater decisions are for licensed or authorised people.

qualityStandard: Each waste stream in the case study is identified and stored in a closed, labelled container, separated from heat sources.
The unapproved discharge in the worked example is stopped, contained and reported, with no product added to any drain.
Each handover to a waste contractor is recorded with the contractor's details and the signature of the person who handed it over.
documentationEvidence: Waste stream log, listing each stream, container, storage place and date.
Containment and incident note for any unapproved discharge, with the time, location and who was told.
Waste collection record with contractor, quantity or number of containers, destination and signatures.
Safety data sheet reference for each product that contributes to the waste stream.
summary: Greasy waste and washwater are fire and contamination hazards, and each waste stream needs its own control.
Keep greasy waste sealed, labelled and away from heat sources until the approved contractor collects it.
Stop an unapproved discharge at source, contain it, and report it. The site operator decides the route.
Record every stream, container, handover and containment, and confirm the lawful route with the site operator.

knowledgeChecks.question: A subcontractor wants to drain greasy washwater into a stormwater grate. What is correct?
options: Drain it, because the grate is nearby and the bucket is heavy
Stop the discharge, contain the water, and tell the site operator at once
Add detergent to the water first, so it drains more easily

knowledgeChecks.question: Who decides the disposal route for greasy waste at a site?
options: The cleaner who did the job, using their own judgement about the bins
The site operator, with a lawful waste contractor, under the approved route
Whichever contractor is cheapest on the day when the bin is full and needs to go

knowledgeChecks.question: How should greasy waste be stored while waiting for collection?
options: Next to the fryer exhaust, so it is easy to load into the van for collection
In open bins in the lane, so that it can be seen by the collector
In closed, labelled containers, away from heat sources and electrical outlets
